a: live as citizens
p: Politeuomai: to live as a citizen of a city. The letter treats the church as a city that needs harmony.
b: The verb politeuomai comes from polis, "city": to take part in public life, to live as a citizen. Paul uses it in Philippians 1:27, where the site has "live as citizens worthy of the good news of Christ" (Philippians 1:27). Clement's whole letter speaks this civic language. Its key words, harmony (homonoia) and rebellion (stasis), are the words Greek and Roman speakers used for a city at peace or a city torn by factions. Here the city is the church, and the citizens are to live in a way worthy of God, who is its ruler.

a: The Spirit of the Lord is a lamp
p: The Hebrew says the human breath is the LORD's lamp. Clement makes the lamp the Lord's Spirit.
b: The saying is Proverbs 20:27. The Hebrew, which the site's Proverbs follows, reads "The human breath is the LORD's lamp, searching through every inner room of the belly" (Proverbs 20:27). The Septuagint has "a light of the Lord is the breath of human beings, which searches the storerooms of the belly." Clement's Greek differs from both: "Spirit of the Lord, a lamp searching the storerooms of the belly." He uses the verse as proof that God sees our hidden thoughts (21:3, 9). "The belly" is the Hebrew picture for the inner self, the place of thoughts and feelings.

a: it says somewhere
p: Clement often quotes Scripture with this loose formula, as Hebrews does, without naming the book.
b: The Greek is legei gar pou, "for it (or he) says somewhere." There is no subject: the speaker is Scripture, or God speaking in it. Clement uses the formula again at 26:2 and, with "the Writing" as subject, at 28:3. Hebrews introduces Psalm 8 the same way: "someone has declared somewhere" (Hebrews 2:6), and Genesis 2:2 with "Somewhere, you see, he spoke about the seventh day like this" (Hebrews 4:4). The vagueness is not ignorance. Clement and his hearers knew the Greek Bible well, and the point is what is said, not where.

a: desert our post
p: Leipotakteō: a soldier's word, to leave one's place in the battle line.
b: Leipotakteō means to leave one's taxis, the rank or post a soldier was given. Clement uses army words often: "deserts" in 28:2 is automoleō, to go over to the enemy, and chapter 37 compares the church to an army in which each man keeps his own rank. The picture fits the letter's purpose. At Corinth some members had pushed out their elders (44:6); Clement calls that leaving the post God assigned.

a: whose blood was given for us
p: Clement speaks of Christ's blood several times; this echoes the words over the cup at the Last Supper.
b: Clement writes "whose blood was given for us" (hyper hēmōn edothē). The words recall the Supper: "This cup is the new covenant, made in my blood. It is being poured out for you" (Luke 22:20). Clement returns to Christ's blood elsewhere: the scarlet cord of Rahab was a sign of it (12:7), and "he gave his blood for us" stands at 49:6. Here the blood is the reason for reverence: the household code that follows begins with the Lord who died for the household.

a: those who are older
p: Presbyteroi can mean older people or the church's elders. Here the list of ages points to age.
b: Presbyteroi is the word for "elders," the church's leaders in 44:5 and 47:6, but it also simply means "older people." Lake translates "the aged" and notes: "Or possibly 'the Presbyters,' but the context makes this improbable." The Plain English Translation agrees. The list moves by age and household: leaders, the older, the young, wives, children (21:6–8), the way Titus 2:2–6 and 1 Peter 5:5 move from older to younger. The leaders (proēgoumenoi, "those who go before us") are named just before, so the office may already be meant there.

a: Let us guide our wives toward what is good
p: 21:6–8 is a household code: duties for each member of the house, addressed here to the men.
b: Chapters 21:6–8 follow the pattern scholars call a household code: instructions for each member of a household in turn, found in Colossians 3:18–4:1, Ephesians 5:21–6:9, 1 Peter 2:18–3:7 and Titus 2:1–10. Clement speaks to the men ("our wives," "our children"), as heads of households, and what he asks of the wives is purity, gentleness, restraint in speech and fair love (21:7). The verb diorthoō means "set straight, correct." Clement praised the Corinthians in 1:3 for once teaching their women this way, so he is calling them back to what they did before the revolt.

a: forbearance
p: Epieikeia is "forbearance" on this site (Titus 3:2); praütēs is "gentleness". Clement pairs them in 30:8.
b: Two Greek words often stand together. Epieikeia is a willingness to yield, to be reasonable and fair rather than insist on one's rights. Praütēs is gentleness or meekness. The site's Titus 3:2 has both: "They should be forbearing and show every kind of gentleness to everyone" (Titus 3:2), so 1 Clement keeps "forbearance" for the first and "gentleness" for the second (21:7; 30:8). Clement calls God himself "forbearing" in 29:1. In a church split by people insisting on their own way, the word is pointed.

a: by their silence
p: Clement asks the wives for a restrained tongue in the household; he does not speak here of the church's meetings.
b: The Greek is "let them make the forbearance of their tongue plain through silence." The point is restraint in speech, the theme of the psalm Clement quotes next ("Keep your tongue away from evil," 22:3) and of the warnings against gossip and slander (30:1–3; 35:5). 1 Peter 3:1–4 likewise hopes wives will win their husbands "without a word." Clement speaks here of character in the household and does not mention the church's meetings. The passages that speak of women's speaking in the assembly are 1 Corinthians 14:34 and 1 Timothy 2:11–12, and the site's card on women in church leadership gives the churches' views.

a: not by favoring one side
p: Prosklisis: leaning toward one party. Clement uses the same word for the Corinthians' old factions (47:3–4).
b: Prosklisis is a leaning toward one side, partiality. The site's 1 Timothy 5:21 has it: "do nothing by leaning to one side" (1 Timothy 5:21). Clement uses the word again in 47:3–4 for the parties at Corinth in Paul's day, who lined up behind Paul, Cephas and Apollos (1 Corinthians 1:12). Even love inside a household can take sides; Clement wants it given "equally" to all who fear God.

a: His breath is in us
p: God gave the breath of life and can take it back: Genesis 2:7, Job 34:14–15 and Psalm 104:29.
b: Clement ends the household code where it began, with God who searches the heart (21:2–3). The breath (pnoē) that God gave is his: "the LORD God shaped the man from dust of the ground and blew into his nostrils the breath of life" (Genesis 2:7). Job 34:14–15 and Psalm 104:29 say that if God drew it back, every living body would die. So the warning is plain: the one who sees our thoughts also holds our life.

a: thoughts and musings
p: The same pair of words as Hebrews 4:12, in reverse order.
b: Clement's ennoiai kai enthymēseis are the two nouns of Hebrews 4:12, where the word of God "sifts and judges the musings and plans of the heart" (Hebrews 4:12). There the order is enthymēseis and ennoiai. 1 Clement echoes Hebrews often, most of all in chapter 36. Here the site renders ennoia "thoughts," as in 21:3, and keeps "musings" from Hebrews.

a: For he himself, through the Holy Spirit, calls us
p: Clement hears Christ speaking Psalm 34 through the Holy Spirit, as Hebrews hears him in the Psalms.
b: "He himself" is Christ, named in the first half of the verse. Clement does not say "David says" but that Christ calls us through the Holy Spirit in the words of Psalm 34. He did the same in 16:15–16, where Christ speaks Psalm 22 in his own person. Hebrews puts psalm verses in Christ's mouth too (Hebrews 2:11–12; 10:5–7), and 1 Peter 1:11 says the Spirit of Christ spoke in the prophets. For Clement the Old Testament is the voice of the Christ who now teaches the church. Jewish readers of the psalm hear David, or the teacher of wisdom calling his pupils "children."

a: Come here, children, and hear me out
p: 22:1–7 is Psalm 34:11–17 almost word for word from the Septuagint; 1 Peter 3:10–12 quotes the same lines.
b: 22:1–7 gives Psalm 34:11–17 (Psalm 33:12–18 in the Greek Bible) close to the Septuagint. Where the Greek agrees with the Hebrew, the Plain English Translation uses the site's wording of the psalm, with "the Lord" for the Greek kyrios, never "the LORD." Where Clement's Greek differs, his wording is translated. He skips 34:18–19 and joins Psalm 32:10 (22:8). 1 Peter 3:10–12 quotes 34:12–16 too, as a call to bless instead of answer insult with insult, and Clement uses it for the same reason: speech that keeps the peace. "Look for peace and run after it" (22:5) is the heart of his letter.

a: The righteous man cried out
p: Clement has the singular, "the righteous man"; the Septuagint and the Hebrew have plural cries.
b: The Septuagint of Psalm 34:17 (33:18) has a plural, "the righteous cried out, and the Lord heard them." The Hebrew has "They cry" (Psalm 34:17). Clement's Greek has the singular: ho dikaios, "the righteous man," and "him" throughout. It may be his own change or the reading of his Greek Bible; a later verse of the psalm, which Clement skips, speaks of one righteous man in the Hebrew (34:19). One Syriac manuscript adds that verse here (see the variant).

a: Many are the whippings of the sinner
p: Clement ends with Psalm 32:10. The Greek has "whips" where the Hebrew has "pains," and "mercy" for loyal love.
b: The last line comes from another psalm, Psalm 32:10 (31:10 in the Greek Bible). The site's Hebrew-based wording is "Pains are many for the wicked; but the one who trusts the LORD, loyal love wraps him around" (Psalm 32:10). The Greek has mastiges, "whips," and eleos, "mercy," the Septuagint's usual word for hesed, the site's "loyal love." The Septuagint has a singular, "the one who hopes"; Clement makes it plural, "those who hope." Joining two psalms by a shared theme was a common Jewish way of reading Scripture.

a: with an undivided mind
p: Haplē dianoia: a single, simple mind, the opposite of the "double-minded" of the next verse.
b: Haplous means single, simple, without folds. Clement sets it against dipsychos, "double-souled, double-minded" (23:2–3). James makes the same contrast: God "gives to everyone with an open hand" (haplōs), but the one who asks must ask "in faith and not waver at all," for "He is a double-minded man, never steady on any road he takes" (James 1:5–8). The Father gives freely to those who come to him with one heart.

a: dream up fancies
p: Indallomai: to appear, to picture. Clement warns against a soul that pictures God's gifts wrongly or doubts them.
b: The verb indallomai means "appear, seem," and in Homer the heart that "pictures" something (LSJ). Lake translates "be fanciful." Clement's sense seems to be a soul that lets its imagination run, either doubting that the promised gifts will come or making them into something they are not. The next verses show which he fears most: people who say the promises have been slow and so will never come (23:3).

a: May this Scripture stay far from us
p: Clement quotes as Scripture words found in no known book. 2 Clement 11:2 quotes them too.
b: Clement calls these words hē graphē, "the Scripture," but they are in no book of the Bible or of the Septuagint. Lake's note: the quotation "which is also found in II. Clem. 11, 2, cannot be identified. Some think it is from the lost apocalypse of Eldad and Modad." 2 Clement introduces it as "the prophetic word" and gives it in a slightly different form. Eldad and Medad are the two men who prophesied in the camp (Numbers 11:26), and the Shepherd of Hermas cites "Eldad and Modat, who prophesied to the people in the wilderness" (Shepherd of Hermas 7:4, Vision 2.3.4); Lake's English calls it "the Book of Eldad and Modat." Lake's note there says the book is named in the Athanasian Synopsis and the Stichometry of Nicephorus but no longer exists. So the guess is possible but unproved. What is clear is that Clement's Bible held words that later churches did not keep.

a: We heard these things back in our fathers' days, too
p: The doubters say God's promises were old news to their fathers and still have not come true.
b: The complaint is the one answered in 2 Peter 3:4, where scoffers ask, "Where is the promise of his coming?" Clement does not say exactly which promises the doubters had in mind. The next verses speak of the Lord's sudden coming (23:5) and then of the resurrection (24–26), so the context points to the hope of Christ's return and the raising of the dead. The vine answers that slowness is not failure: growth takes stages, but the fruit comes.

a: Compare yourselves to a tree
p: Each stage of the vine is slow, but the grapes come. So God's promises will ripen.
b: The vine sheds its leaves, buds, leafs, flowers, sets a hard sour grape (omphax) and at last a ripe cluster. Jesus used the fig tree the same way: "When its branch is already soft and it pushes out its leaves, you know that summer is close" (Matthew 24:32). The quotation probably ends with the ripe cluster, as Lake prints it, and Clement then draws the lesson in his own voice: "in a short time" the fruit is ripe. 2 Clement 11:4 applies the same vine to God's people, who will have troubles first and then receive good things.

a: He will come quickly and will not delay
p: A line of the Greek Isaiah 13:22, which in the Hebrew speaks of Babylon's doom coming near.
b: Lake's margin points to Isaiah 13:22 in the Septuagint, which ends "it comes quickly and will not delay" (tachy erchetai kai ou chroniei). There the subject is the doom of Babylon; the site's Hebrew-based Isaiah reads "Its time is near, it is coming; its days will not be drawn out" (Isaiah 13:22). Clement makes "he" the subject and turns a word of judgment into a promise of the Lord's coming. Hebrews 10:37, drawing on Habakkuk 2:3, makes the same promise: "the one who is coming will come, and he will not be late" (Hebrews 10:37).

a: and the Holy One whom you are waiting for
p: Malachi has "the messenger of the covenant"; Clement's Greek has "the Holy One."
b: The second quotation is Malachi 3:1. The site's Malachi reads "Then all at once the Lord you are looking for will come to his temple. The messenger of the covenant, whom you delight in, look, he is coming" (Malachi 3:1). The Septuagint is close to that. Clement's form joins the two halves with "and" and puts "the Holy One" (ho hagios) where Malachi has "the messenger (angelos) of the covenant." He does not say whether "the Lord" and "the Holy One" are one figure or two. The Gospels apply the first half of the verse to John the Baptist as the one sent ahead (Mark 1:2). Clement uses it of the Lord's coming at the end.

a: its firstfruits
p: As in 1 Corinthians 15:20: the risen Christ is the first part of a harvest still to come.
b: Clement follows Paul, writing to the same city forty years earlier: "Christ has been raised from the dead, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep" (1 Corinthians 15:20). The firstfruits (aparchē) were the first of the harvest, given to God as a pledge that the rest would follow (Leviticus 23:10–11). Clement's proofs of the resurrection in 24–26 also follow 1 Corinthians 15: the seed sown in the ground (24:4–5; 1 Corinthians 15:36–38). He wants the Corinthians to hear their own letter from Paul again (47:1).

a: The night goes to sleep, and the day rises
p: The verbs are the words for death and resurrection: "fall asleep" and "rise."
b: Clement chooses his verbs with care. Koimaomai, "sleep," is the New Testament's gentle word for the death of believers ("those who have fallen asleep," 1 Corinthians 15:20). Anistamai, "rise," is the verb of resurrection, from which anastasis comes. So every night and morning acts out a death and a rising. It is a picture, not an argument from nature alone: Clement has already named its pattern, Christ raised from the dead (24:1).

a: Let us take the crops
p: Paul (1 Corinthians 15:36–38) and Jesus (John 12:24) use the seed as a picture of resurrection.
b: "The sower went out" (24:5) uses the opening words of the parable of the sower (Mark 4:3; Matthew 13:3). But the lesson is Paul's: "What you sow does not come alive unless it dies" and "You sow a bare grain" (1 Corinthians 15:36–37). Clement's seeds fall "dry and bare" and "break down" before God raises them. Jesus said of his own death, "if a grain of wheat does not fall into the earth and die, it remains a single grain" (John 12:24). Clement leaves out Paul's point that the new body differs from the seed.

a: the Master's providence
p: Pronoia, "forethought," was the philosophers' word for God's care of the world. Wisdom of Solomon uses it too.
b: Pronoia is "forethought," care that plans ahead. Greek thinkers used it for the divine ordering of the world. It is rare in the Greek Bible: Wisdom of Solomon calls on God, "your providence, Father, is at the helm" (Wisdom of Solomon 14:3) and speaks of "the providence that never ends" (Wisdom of Solomon 17:2). Clement speaks of the "majesty" of this care: the God who planned the world raises the seed. It is the same Master who orders the heavens in chapter 20.
r: Wisdom of Solomon 14:3; Wisdom of Solomon 17:2; 20:1–11

a: the strange sign
p: Herodotus told of the phoenix 500 years before Clement; Pliny and others repeated it. Clement's form is his own.
b: Lake notes: "The same story, with variations, is found in Herodotus (ii. 73), Pliny (Nat. Hist. x. 2), etc." Herodotus, in the 400s BC, heard at Heliopolis that the bird comes from Arabia once in five hundred years, when its parent dies, and brings the parent to the temple of the Sun inside a ball of myrrh. He says he saw it only in pictures and did not find the story believable. Clement's version is different: the dying bird builds a tomb of spices, a worm grows out of its body into the new bird, and the priests check their records (25:2–5). The word "phoenix" (phoinix) also meant the date palm, and Lake adds that Christians found the bird in the Greek Psalm 92:12, where dikaios hōs phoinix anthēsei can be read "the righteous will flourish like a phoenix" as well as "like a palm."

a: the only one of its kind
p: Monogenēs: the same word John uses for Jesus, the "only" Son.
b: Monogenēs means "the only one of its kind," the single member of its family. It is the word of John 3:16, "he gave his only Son" (John 3:16), and of John 1:14. Clement does not draw the link here; he uses the word because there is only ever one phoenix alive at a time.

a: a tomb
p: Sēkos: a pen, a shrine, a tomb. It is also the thing the young bird carries to Egypt.
b: Sēkos first meant a pen or fold for young animals, then a sacred enclosure or shrine, and also a sepulchre (LSJ). Lake has "sepulchre." The Plain English Translation says "tomb," because the bird dies in it and the bones of the old bird are carried in it (25:3). In Herodotus's version the young bird carries its parent in a ball of myrrh; Clement's "tomb" made of spices plays the same part.

a: Heliopolis
p: The Egyptian city the Bible calls On, home of the sun god's temple, near modern Cairo.
b: Heliopolis, Greek for "City of the Sun," was one of Egypt's oldest holy cities, the center of the sun god's worship, near modern Cairo. The Hebrew Bible calls it On: Joseph married Asenath, "the daughter of Potiphera, priest of On" (Genesis 41:45), and the Septuagint there translates On as "Heliopolis." Herodotus also heard the phoenix story from the priests of this city. Clement's "altar of the sun" (25:4) and "the priests" (25:5) belong to the sun god's temple there.

a: the records of the years
t: Did Clement think the phoenix was real?
p: Clement tells it as a fact of nature, as many ancient writers did. No such bird exists.
b: Clement tells the story as something that happens ("the strange sign that takes place"), checked in the priests' records, and he draws from it a proof that the Creator can raise the dead (26:1). Nothing in the chapter suggests he took it for a fable. Ancient natural history reported it, though Herodotus himself had doubted it. Tertullian later used the same bird for the resurrection of the flesh and read Psalm 92:12 as "The righteous shall flourish like the phœnix" (On the Resurrection of the Flesh 13). Verdict: the bird is a legend; Clement's argument rests on it, but his faith in the resurrection rests on Christ (24:1) and Scripture (26:2–3), which follow.

a: And you will raise me up, and I will give you thanks
t: A psalm line not found as given
p: No psalm has these words exactly. Lake's margin points to Psalm 28:7, whose Greek speaks of flesh blooming again.
b: No verse of the Greek or Hebrew Psalms reads "And you will raise me up, and I will give you thanks." Lake's margin points to Psalm 28:7. In the Septuagint (Psalm 27:7) that verse says "my flesh has bloomed again, and from my will I will give thanks to him"; the site's Hebrew-based wording ends "I will thank him out of my song" (Psalm 28:7). The second line is Psalm 3:5, "I lay down and fell asleep; I woke up" (Psalm 3:5); where the Hebrew goes on "for the LORD was holding me," Clement has "for you are with me," close to Psalm 23:4.

a: this flesh of mine
p: Clement reads Job 19:26 as the raising of the flesh. The Greek has "skin," the Hebrew "from my flesh I will see God."
b: The Septuagint of Job 19:26 has "may he raise up my skin that endures these things." Clement's Greek says "you will raise up this flesh of mine," with "flesh" (sarx) for "skin" and the line turned into a promise to God. The site's Hebrew-based wording is "Even after my skin has been stripped off like this, from my flesh I will see God" (Job 19:26). The site's Job 19 page notes that from 1 Clement 26:3 on, Christians read 19:25–27 as a prophecy of the resurrection of the body. Clement wants the Corinthians to hope for the raising of the very body that suffered.

a: nothing is impossible with God except lying
p: A sharp twist on "nothing is impossible with God": the one thing God cannot do is lie.
b: Clement takes the famous saying that nothing is impossible for God (Luke 1:37; Genesis 18:14) and adds the one exception: lying. Hebrews 6:18 speaks of two unchangeable things "where it is impossible that God would lie," and Titus 1:2 of "The God who does not lie" (Titus 1:2). The argument is from the lesser to the greater: the God who commanded people not to lie will surely not lie himself. So his promise of the resurrection (26:1) can be trusted.

a: be kindled again
p: Anazōpyreō: to stir a fire back into flame, the verb of 2 Timothy 1:6.
b: Anazōpyreō is to rekindle embers into a flame. Paul tells Timothy, "stir up the fire of God's gift again" (2 Timothy 1:6). Clement's faith is not dead but low, like a fire that needs stirring, and the thing that stirs it is the memory of God's faithfulness (27:1–2).

a: Who will say to him, 'What have you done?'
p: The question is in Wisdom of Solomon 12:12, a book that Catholic and Orthodox Bibles include.
b: Lake's margin points to Wisdom of Solomon 12:12, which the site translates "Who will say, "What have you done?" Or who will stand against your judgment?" (Wisdom of Solomon 12:12). Clement's second line differs: "the might of his strength" instead of "your judgment." Similar questions stand in Job 9:12, Ecclesiastes 8:4 and Daniel 4:35. Clement gives no formula here, so it is not clear that he means to quote a book at all. Wisdom of Solomon is in Catholic and Orthodox Bibles; Protestant churches and Judaism do not count it as Scripture.
r: Wisdom of Solomon 12:12; Job 9:12; Daniel 4:35; Romans 9:20

a: not one of the things he has decreed will pass away
p: Like Jesus' "my words will never be gone": what God has decided will stand.
b: The Greek ou mē parelthē, "will by no means pass away," is the strong negative Jesus uses: "Heaven and earth will be gone, but my words will never be gone" (Matthew 24:35). Clement applies it to God's decrees, which here include the promise of the resurrection. The whole chapter answers the doubters of 23:3: God's word made the world (27:4) and his word does not fail.

a: no words and no speeches whose voices are not heard
t: The Greek Psalm 19:3: every voice is heard
p: The Hebrew line can be read as silence or as a voice heard everywhere. The Greek, which Clement quotes, has the second sense.
b: Clement quotes Psalm 19:1–3 (18:2–4 in the Greek). For the first two lines the site's Hebrew-based wording fits his Greek and is used. The third line is read two ways. Word for word the Hebrew says "there is no speech and there are no words; their voice is not heard." The site's Psalm 19 takes it as silence: "No speech, no words; no voice of theirs is heard" (Psalm 19:3), as do the ASV and Young's Literal Translation. The King James Version supplies a word and reads it the other way: "There is no speech nor language, where their voice is not heard." The Septuagint, which Clement quotes, has the second sense plainly: "There are no speeches nor words whose voices are not heard." Clement needs that sense: nothing escapes God, and his works speak to all. Paul quotes the next verse, "Their voice has gone out into the whole earth" (Romans 10:18).
orig: οὐκ εἰσὶν λόγοι οὐδὲ λαλιαί (ouk eisin logoi oude laliai)

a: anyone who deserts him
p: Automoleō: to go over to the enemy. Clement keeps up his army picture (21:4; 37).
b: Automoleō means to desert, to go over to the other side in a war. With "desert our post" (21:4) and the army of chapter 37, it makes the revolt at Corinth a soldier's betrayal. The question has an answer in the psalm that follows: there is no world beyond God's reach for a deserter to run to.

a: the Writing
p: Grapheion: a rare word for Scripture. Its usual senses are a pen or a record office.
b: Clement usually says hē graphē, "the Scripture" (23:3; 34:6; 35:7). Here he writes to grapheion, a rare word whose ordinary senses are a pencil or brush, a registry or record office (LSJ). Lake translates "the Writing." In context it plainly means Scripture, and what follows is a psalm.

a: Where will I go, and where will I hide from your face?
p: Clement gives Psalm 139:7–10 loosely, with "the depths" where the psalm has Sheol, the world of the dead.
b: The words follow Psalm 139:7–10 freely. The site's Hebrew-based wording is "Should I climb to the heavens, you are there; should I make Sheol my bed, here you are" (Psalm 139:8). Clement has "the farthest ends of the earth" and "the depths" (abyssoi), where the psalm has the far side of the sea and Sheol, and he moves "your spirit" from the first line of the psalm to the last. The order and words differ from both the Hebrew and the Septuagint. The point is the psalm's: there is nowhere to run from God.

a: lifting up pure and spotless hands
p: Jews and early Christians prayed standing with hands lifted up. Clement asks that the hands be clean.
b: Raised hands were the ordinary posture of prayer in Israel and the early church (Psalm 141:2; Lamentations 2:19). 1 Timothy 2:8 asks "that in every place the men pray with holy hands raised, free of anger and argument" (1 Timothy 2:8), and the link to quarreling is the same as Clement's. Clean hands mean a clean life (Psalm 24:3–4). A church in revolt cannot lift pure hands.

a: a chosen portion
p: God's people as the share he chose for himself, like Israel in Deuteronomy 32:9.
b: "Portion" (meros, and meris in 29:2 and 30:1) is a share of land or of an inheritance. In Deuteronomy 32:9 Israel is the LORD's share, chosen out of all the nations. Clement applies the picture to the church: God chose "us" as his portion. He does not say Israel has lost its place; he reads the promise as now including the Gentile Christians of Rome and Corinth (64:1 speaks of "a people of his own").

a: the number of the angels of God
p: The Septuagint sets the nations by the number of God's angels; the site's Deuteronomy has "the sons of God."
b: Clement quotes Deuteronomy 32:8–9 from the Septuagint, which says the Most High set the nations' borders "by the number of the angels of God." The Masoretic Text has "the sons of Israel"; a Dead Sea Scroll has "the sons of God," which the site's Deuteronomy follows: "to match the number of the sons of God" (Deuteronomy 32:8). The variant entry there explains why. In this picture the nations were given to heavenly beings, but the Lord kept his people for himself. The Greek also says God "scattered" the children of Adam, the word the Greek Genesis uses at Babel: "The LORD scattered them from there" (Genesis 11:8). The Hebrew of Deuteronomy 32:8 says he "split up" the children of Adam.

a: Look, the Lord is taking for himself a nation
t: A quotation from no known book
p: No book has these words. Lake: several verses resemble them, but Clement may use a lost source.
b: Clement introduces these words as Scripture ("in another place it says"), but they match no known text. Lake's margin lists Deuteronomy 4:34 and 14:2 (God takes a nation from among the nations; Israel is his treasured people), Numbers 18:27 and 2 Chronicles 31:14 (the firstfruits of the threshing floor) and Ezekiel 48:12 (a most holy portion). His note: these "most nearly resemble this quotation, but the difference is considerable, and Clement may be referring to some lost source." As at 23:3, his Bible was not quite ours.

a: the most holy things
p: Hagia hagiōn: the phrase for the Most Holy Place and for the most holy offerings.
b: The Greek hagia hagiōn, "holy things of holy things," is the Septuagint's phrase for what is most holy: the inner room of the sanctuary and the priests' share of the offerings (Numbers 18:9). Lake capitalizes it, "the Holy of Holies." In the quotation the nation is God's firstfruits, and the most holy things come from it as the best of a harvest is set apart for God. Clement does not explain further. He draws only the lesson that a people so chosen must live in holiness (30:1).

a: uprisings
p: Neōterismos: an attempt at change, a revolt. Lake took it as "youthful lusts."
b: Neōterismos comes from neōteros, "newer, younger." Its usual sense is "innovation" in politics, a revolutionary movement (LSJ, citing Plato and Demosthenes). Lake translates "youthful lusts," taking the word from "young." In a list of sins this could mean either, but the letter is about a revolt in which younger men rose against their elders (3:3), so the political sense fits Clement's theme. The Plain English Translation says "uprisings," and keeps "rebellion" for stasis.

a: God takes his stand against the proud
t: Proverbs 3:34 as James and 1 Peter give it
p: Clement's Greek is the form of James 4:6 and 1 Peter 5:5, with "God" where the Septuagint has "the Lord."
b: The saying is Proverbs 3:34. The Hebrew reads "Mockers he mocks, but the humble he gives his favor" (Proverbs 3:34). The Septuagint has "The Lord takes his stand against the proud, but to the humble he gives grace." James 4:6 and 1 Peter 5:5 quote it with "God" for "the Lord," and so does Clement. So the site's New Testament wording is used: "God takes his stand against the proud, but to the humble he gives grace" (James 4:6). 1 Peter uses it, like Clement, in a call to submit to elders (1 Peter 5:5).

a: be justified by works, not by words
p: Clement says this here and in 32:4 that we are justified through faith, not works. Lightfoot reads the two as a deliberate balance.
b: Clement's contrast is works against words: a faith that only talks, set against a faith that acts. James makes the same contrast and uses the same verb: "So you see that it is by works that a person is justified, and not by faith alone" (James 2:24). Two chapters later Clement says Christians "are not justified through ourselves ... or through works we have done in holiness of heart, but through faith" (32:4). Lightfoot (1890, note on chapter 33) sees a "studied effort to keep the balance": after "declaring emphatically that men are not justified by their own works but by faith," Clement "hastens to balance this statement by urging the importance of good works." Clement himself does not explain how the two sayings fit. The chapter 32 page says more, and the site's cards at Romans 3, James 2 and Joshua 2 give the churches' answers.

a: The one who says a lot will hear a lot in reply
p: Zophar's words to Job, from the Septuagint, which differs much from the Hebrew here.
b: These lines are Job 11:2–3 in the Septuagint, from Zophar's first speech to Job. The Greek reads close to Clement's words. The Hebrew is different: "Is no one going to answer all these words? Will a man who is all talk win his case?" (Job 11:2). Clement uses Zophar as Scripture for one point only: much talk is not righteousness. He will quote Job's friend Eliphaz the same way in chapter 39.

a: Blessed is the one born of a woman who lives a short life
p: Lake: "The text is here obviously corrupt; but the corruption is in the LXX, not in Clement."
b: The Greek reads "blessed, born of woman, short-lived," which makes little sense. The Septuagint of Job 11:3 has the same words, so Lake's note says: "The text is here obviously corrupt; but the corruption is in the LXX, not in Clement." The same words, "born of a woman, short-lived," open the Greek Job 14:1, where they make sense; somewhere in the Greek tradition they seem to have come into Job 11:3 as well. Clement quotes his Bible faithfully, odd line and all.
orig: εὐλογημένος γεννητὸς γυναικὸς ὀλιγόβιος (eulogēmenos gennētos gynaikos oligobios)

a: as it was given to our fathers, the righteous
p: Like Hebrews 11, which says the people of old "were given a good witness" by faith.
b: The "testimony" (martyria) Clement means is the good report God and others gave of the righteous of old. Hebrews 11 uses the same family of words: "It was by faith that the people of long ago were given a good witness" (Hebrews 11:2). Clement's own lists of examples (chapters 4–12, 17–18, 31) work the same way as Hebrews 11, and in 17:1 he speaks of the prophets and of "those who were given testimony."

a: he did righteousness and truth through faith
p: Clement names faith, as Genesis 15:6 and Romans 4 do, and a life of righteousness, as James 2 does.
b: Abraham's blessing came because he "did righteousness and truth through faith." Both halves matter to Clement. Paul stresses the faith: "Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness" (Romans 4:3). James stresses the deeds: "his faith was at work along with his works" (James 2:22). Earlier Clement praised Abraham for obedience (10:1–2) and for faith and hospitality (10:7). Here, in a chapter about humility, the point is that the blessing was God's gift to one who trusted him.

a: he was gladly led up to be a sacrifice
p: Clement makes Isaac a willing sacrifice who knew the outcome, as 4 Maccabees does.
b: Genesis 22 says nothing of Isaac's feelings. Clement says he knew "with confidence" what would come and went "gladly." A Jewish retelling of the Greek period also made Isaac a willing offering: in 4 Maccabees the martyrs remember "by whose fatherly hand Isaac was willing to be slaughtered for godliness" (4 Maccabees 13:12). Hebrews 11:17–19 says Abraham reckoned that God could raise the dead. For Clement, Isaac's "confidence" is the same trust in God's promise he asks of the Corinthians.

a: the scepter of the twelve tribes of Israel
p: Dōdekaskēptron: a rare word, "twelve-scepter," the rule over Israel's twelve tribes.
b: Clement coins or uses a rare compound, dōdekaskēptron, "the twelve-scepter." A scepter was the staff of a tribe's ruler, and in Hebrew the same word (shevet) means both "scepter" and "tribe." So Jacob received the rule of the twelve tribes that came from his sons. In 32:2 Clement goes on to "his other scepters," the tribes other than Levi and Judah. Jacob's flight "because of his brother" is Genesis 27:41–28:5, and his service to Laban Genesis 29–31; Clement calls it humility.

a: the gifts are that he gave
p: Lake: "by him" in 32:1 means God; "from him" in 32:2 means Jacob.
b: Lake's note: "The obscurity of this passage is partly due to an ambiguity in the Greek, partly to the faultiness of the chapter-divisions. The first verse of this chapter ought really to be closely connected with the last verse of Chapter XXXI; the 'by him' in XXXII, 1 means 'by God,' and the 'from him' in XXXII, 2 means from Jacob." So the gifts are God's, and the line of priests, kings and the Lord Jesus comes from Jacob.

a: From him, in his human descent, comes the Lord Jesus
p: The same Greek phrase as Romans 9:5: Christ comes from Israel's fathers "according to the flesh."
b: The words to kata sarka, "as to the flesh," are the words of Romans 9:5: "from them, in his human descent, comes the Christ" (Romans 9:5). Paul lists Israel's gifts; Clement lists the gifts that came through Jacob: the priests and Levites, the Lord Jesus, and the kings of Judah. Like Paul, he puts Jesus in the middle of Israel's story, and the phrase implies there is more to Christ than his human descent.

a: like the stars of the sky
p: The promise of Genesis 15:5, 22:17 and 26:4.
b: God promised Abraham offspring like the stars (Genesis 15:5; 22:17) and repeated it to Isaac: "I will make your offspring as many as the stars of the sky" (Genesis 26:4). Clement's short form is close to the Septuagint of these verses. He uses the promise to show that the whole people's glory came from God's word, not their own effort (32:3).

a: are not justified through ourselves
p: Close to Paul's "justified by faith." Lightfoot reads it with 30:3 and 33:1 as a deliberate balance of Paul and James.
b: Clement says Christians are justified "not through ourselves": not through wisdom, understanding, godliness, or even works done "in holiness of heart," but through faith. The words echo Romans 3:28 ("a person is justified by faith, apart from works of the law") and Ephesians 2:8–9 ("This does not come from you"). Yet Clement goes straight on to good works (33:1) and has just said "justified by works, not by words" (30:3). Lightfoot (1890) calls 32:4 an emphatic statement "that men are not justified by their own works but by faith," which Clement at once balances "by urging the importance of good works," and he links that balance to Clement's place in a Roman church of Jewish and Gentile Christians. The chapter page says more; the site's cards at Romans 3, James 2 and Joshua 2 give the churches' answers.

a: all those from the beginning of time
p: Pantas tous ap' aiōnos: all those since time began, justified through faith. The Greek does not say "all people."
b: The Greek is "all those from the age," that is, since time began. Lake: "all men from the beginning of the world." The Plain English Translation keeps the Greek's open "all those." Clement means that God has always justified people in one way, through faith, from Abel and Enoch onward, the line of Hebrews 11. He does not say whether every human being is meant or all the righteous of every age; the examples he has given (Abraham, Isaac, Jacob) suggest the second.
orig: πάντας τοὺς ἀπ᾽ αἰῶνος (pantas tous ap' aiōnos)

a: So what are we to do, brothers?
p: Clement asks Paul's question in Romans 6:1: if we are justified by faith, may we stop doing good?
b: Paul asked, "So what will we say? Should we stay in sin so that grace may multiply?" (Romans 6:1), and answered with a strong "No!" Clement asks the same kind of question about faith and good works and gives the same kind of answer (mēthamōs, "by no means"). Being justified through faith (32:4) is not a reason to be idle; it is the start of eager work, because God himself works and rejoices in his works (33:2).

a: then shut it in by his own power
p: God sets limits for the sea, as in Job 38:8–11 and Psalm 104:9.
b: Clement retells creation in order: the heavens, the earth separated from the waters, the animals, the sea and its creatures, and last the human being (33:3–4). The sea "shut in" by God's power is a biblical picture: God asks Job, "Who closed doors to hold back the sea" (Job 38:8) and set a boundary it may not cross (Psalm 104:9; Jeremiah 5:22). Clement drew the same picture in 20:6–7.

a: as the stamp of his own image
p: Charaktēr: an impression stamped on a coin or seal. Hebrews 1:3 calls the Son the stamp of God's being.
b: Charaktēr is the mark a die leaves on a coin or a seal on wax. Clement says God formed the human being as the stamp of his own image (Genesis 1:26–27). Hebrews uses the word of the Son: "the exact stamp of his being" (Hebrews 1:3). Clement will quote that very passage of Hebrews in 36:2. He also says God shaped humankind "with his holy and faultless hands," the picture of Genesis 2:7, where God shapes the man from the ground.

a: Let us make humankind in our image and likeness
p: Clement quotes Genesis 1 from the Septuagint, shortened. He adds that God "praised" his works.
b: Clement gives Genesis 1:26–27 and 1:28 from the Greek, leaving out the rule over fish, birds and animals. The site's Genesis reads "Let us make humankind in our image, as our likeness" (Genesis 1:26), and the Greek says "made" where the site's Hebrew-based text says "created." Clement's "he praised them" (33:6) is his own word for Genesis 1:31: "God looked at everything he had made, and there it was, very good" (Genesis 1:31). His point is that God delighted in good works, so we should too.

a: the Lord himself adorned himself with good works
p: "The Lord" may be God, adorned by his works of creation, or Christ, who went about doing good.
b: In context "the Lord" seems to be God the Creator: the chapter is about his works (33:2–6) and his joy in them, and the righteous follow his "model to trace" (33:8). Lightfoot (1890) takes it so, because of the "so" and "was glad," read with God's rejoicing in 33:2. Clement also calls Jesus "the Lord" (21:6; 24:1), and the title by itself would fit Christ, whose life was full of good deeds (Acts 10:38).

a: this model to trace
p: Hypogrammos: the model letters a child traces in learning to write.
b: A hypogrammos was a writing copy, the line of letters a teacher wrote for a child to copy or trace (LSJ). The site's 1 Peter 2:21 has "a model to trace" (1 Peter 2:21), and 1 Clement keeps it in all three places. Clement uses the word three times: for Paul's endurance (5:7), for the Lord's humility (16:17), and here for God's own joy in good works. The Christian life is copying a teacher's hand.

a: The good worker
p: The worker who earns his bread can face his employer; the lazy one cannot.
b: Clement uses a picture from daily life, like Jesus' saying "A worker has earned his pay," which 1 Timothy 5:18 quotes as Scripture: "A worker has earned his pay" (1 Timothy 5:18). "With his head held high" translates meta parrēsias, the frank freedom of someone with nothing to hide. The site's usual rendering, "freedom of speech" (as Acts 2:29, "I can speak freely to you"), is kept where speech is in view (35:2, "truth with freedom of speech"); here no one speaks, so the English gives the worker's open face. The lazy worker "does not look in the face" (antophthalmei) the one who hired him. So Christians who do good can face God at his coming (34:3).

a: Look, here is the Lord, and his reward goes ahead of him
p: Clement blends Isaiah 40:10 and 62:11 with Proverbs 24:12. Revelation 22:12 makes the same blend.
b: Clement's words are built from Isaiah 40:10 and 62:11 ("Look, he brings his reward with him, and his wages go ahead of him," Isaiah 62:11) and from the end of Proverbs 24:12, God will pay each person by what he has done. Revelation 22:12 makes the same blend in Jesus' mouth: "Look, I am coming soon, and my reward is with me, to pay each person back for the work they have done" (Revelation 22:12). Clement's "before his face" (pro prosōpou autou) is the Greek of Isaiah 62:11.

a: in any good work
p: The phrase of Titus 3:1, which Lake's margin gives here and at 33:1.
b: Lake's margin points to Titus 3:1, where believers are told "to stand ready for any good work" (Titus 3:1). Titus 3:5 had just said God saved us "not on the basis of works we ourselves had done." Titus and Clement share the same order of thought: saved by God's mercy, then eager for good works (32:4–33:1). Whether Clement knew Titus is debated, since the phrase could come from common Christian teaching.

a: Tens of thousands of tens of thousands
p: Clement joins Daniel 7:10 and Isaiah 6:3, and says "all creation" where Isaiah says "the earth."
b: Clement joins two visions of the heavenly court. The first half is Daniel 7:10, where the site has "Thousands upon thousands waited on him, and tens of thousands of tens of thousands were standing before him" (Daniel 7:10). Clement puts the tens of thousands first and uses the verb "served" (leitourgeō, the verb of worship services) found in Theodotion's Greek Daniel. The second half is the seraphs' cry of Isaiah 6:3, with "all creation" (ktisis) for Isaiah's "earth." "The Lord of Armies" renders kyrios sabaōth, as the site does in Romans 9:29.

a: gathered together in one place
t: The church joins the angels' song?
p: The gathered church cries out "as if from one mouth": an early hint of the "Holy, holy, holy" in worship?
b: "In one place" is epi to auto, the phrase the New Testament uses for the church gathered: "they were all gathered together in the same place" (Acts 2:1); "when you meet together in one place" (1 Corinthians 11:20). Right after the angels' "Holy, holy, holy," Clement calls the assembled church to cry out to God with one voice. The site's Isaiah 6:3 note calls this a use of the angels' song in Christian worship "already hinted at." The text itself does not say that the Roman church sang Isaiah's words; it says the church should pray as one, the way the angels serve God together. Lake notes that "others translate 'in concord and a good conscience,'" but he doubts the Greek allows it.

a: No eye has seen
p: Clement quotes Paul's text but ends "for those who wait for him," as Isaiah 64:4 does.
b: Clement's words follow 1 Corinthians 2:9: "What no eye has seen and no ear has heard, and what has not come up into a human heart, all that God has prepared for those who love him" (1 Corinthians 2:9). But he ends "for those who wait for him," the ending of Isaiah 64:4 ("one who acts for those who wait for him," Isaiah 64:4). He also has "the Lord" where Paul has "God" (see the variant). The site's 1 Corinthians note lists 1 Clement 34:8 among the other early forms of the saying. Clement uses it to make waiting itself a virtue (35:3–4).

a: Father of the ages
p: A title for God as Lord of all time. Clement calls him "King of the ages" in 61:2.
b: "The ages" (aiōnes) are the long spans of time, and also the world itself through time. "Father of the ages" is a rare title; Clement calls God "King of the ages" in his prayer (61:2), as 1 Timothy 1:17 does. Here the title fits the question: only the one who rules all of time knows what he has prepared for the time to come.

a: all unrighteousness and wickedness, greed
t: A list of vices from Romans 1
p: Clement's list is close to Paul's in Romans 1:29–30, and 35:6 takes its last line.
b: Clement's list is close to Paul's in Romans 1:29–30, though not word for word. Five words are the same and have the site's renderings: unrighteousness, wickedness, greed, deceit and spite. Where Paul names kinds of people, "They whisper behind backs" (Romans 1:29), "they slander, they hate God, they are insolent, proud and boastful" (Romans 1:30), Clement has the matching nouns: gossip (psithyrismoi, as in 30:3), slander, hatred of God, pride and arrogance. Paul's eris is "strife" in the site's Romans; here it is "fights," as the letter renders eris "fighting" throughout. Clement adds two of his own at the end, "empty glory-seeking" and "lack of hospitality." The next verse (35:6) takes Paul's last line, that God condemns not only those who do such things but those who approve.

a: those who applaud them
p: The end of Romans 1:32: approving evil is as bad as doing it.
b: Paul ends his list: "they do these things themselves, and they also applaud others who do them" (Romans 1:32). The verb is the same (syneudokeō). For Clement the point is close to home: at Corinth a few led the revolt (47:6), but many went along with it. Those who applauded share the guilt.

a: But to the sinner God said
p: 35:7–12 is Psalm 50:16–23 from the Septuagint, which differs from the Hebrew in several lines.
b: Clement quotes Psalm 50:16–23 (49:16–23 in the Greek) almost exactly as the Septuagint has it. The site's Psalm is made from the Hebrew, which differs: "But God says to the wicked" (Psalm 50:16) where the Greek has "to the sinner"; "You hate to be taught a lesson" (Psalm 50:17); "Understand this, you who forget God, or I will rip you to pieces, and no one will save you" (Psalm 50:22). The last verse differs most: the Greek has "a sacrifice of praise will glorify me, and there is the way by which I will show him the salvation of God." The Plain English Translation follows Clement's Greek, using the site's words where they fit. The psalm is God's charge against people who recite his covenant but slander their brothers, which is what Clement charges the rebels with.

a: like a lion
p: Clement's Greek adds "like a lion." It is not in the Septuagint as Swete and Rahlfs print it, nor in the Hebrew.
b: The Septuagint of Psalm 50:22 (49:22), as printed by Swete and by Rahlfs, reads "lest he snatch, and there be no one to rescue." Clement's Greek adds hōs leōn, "like a lion." The Hebrew has "or I will rip you to pieces" (Psalm 50:22), the verb used of a lion or wild animal tearing its prey (Psalm 7:2). The addition may come from Clement's own copy of the Greek psalm or from his memory of similar lines. Either way it makes the warning vivid.

a: A sacrifice of praise
p: The Greek psalm's phrase, which Hebrews 13:15 uses for Christian worship.
b: "A sacrifice of praise" (thysia aineseōs) is the Septuagint's wording for the thank offering of Psalm 50:23. Hebrews takes it up: "So through him let us keep bringing up to God a sacrifice of praise, the fruit of lips that confess his name" (Hebrews 13:15). Clement links "the way" of this verse to Christ in 36:1: the way in which God shows his salvation is Jesus Christ, "the high priest of our offerings."

a: the high priest of our offerings
p: Clement, like Hebrews, calls Jesus "high priest." He presents the church's offerings to God.
b: Of the New Testament books, only Hebrews calls Jesus "high priest" (Hebrews 2:17; 3:1; 4:14–15). Clement uses the title three times (36:1; 61:3; 64:1), and here he says Christ is high priest "of our offerings" (prosphorai). Clement does not say what the offerings are. In 40–44 he speaks of the Temple's offerings and of elders who "presented the gifts" (44:4). How the churches understand those offerings is on the site's cards at Hebrews 7 (an ordained priesthood) and Hebrews 10 (the Eucharist as sacrifice).

a: protector
p: Prostatēs: a patron or champion who stands up for those weaker than himself.
b: A prostatēs was a protector, a patron who stood up for others in court or public life. Paul calls Phoebe a prostatis: "She has been a patron to many people" (Romans 16:2). Clement calls Christ the protector and helper "of our weakness," close to Hebrews 4:15, where the high priest is able "to feel for us in our weaknesses."

a: we see, as in a mirror
p: Through Christ we see God's face as in a mirror, as in 2 Corinthians 3:18.
b: Enoptrizomai is to see as in a mirror (enoptron). Paul writes: "All of us, our faces uncovered, gaze at the glory of the Lord as in a mirror" (2 Corinthians 3:18), and "For now we look through a mirror, and what we see is a riddle" (1 Corinthians 13:12). The Greek says "his" face; the Plain English Translation says "God's," since Christ is the one through whom we see. The five clauses beginning "through him" are a hymn-like run of praise, and the eyes opened and the mind lit up recall Ephesians 1:18 and 4:18.

a: He is the brightness that shines out from God's majesty
p: 36:2–5 follows Hebrews 1:3–13 closely: the same psalms in the same order, and some of the same words.
b: Clement gives Hebrews 1:3–4 in his own words and then, like Hebrews 1:5–13, quotes Psalm 104:4, Psalm 2:7 and Psalm 110:1. Where Hebrews has "the brightness that shines out from God's glory" (Hebrews 1:3), Clement has "of his majesty"; where Hebrews says the Son "became better than the angels" (Hebrews 1:4), Clement says he "is greater." He does not name Hebrews. Eusebius noticed the link: Clement "gives many thoughts drawn from the Epistle to the Hebrews," quoting some words exactly, which proves Hebrews was not a recent work; some, he says, thought Clement himself had translated Hebrews (Church History 3.38.1–3). Lightfoot (1890) agrees that the passage "is borrowed from the opening of the Epistle to the Hebrews." The site's Hebrews introduction dates Hebrews "before about AD 96, when 1 Clement ... echoes it."

a: He makes his angels into winds
p: The same Greek as Hebrews 1:7, so the site's Hebrews wording is used.
b: Clement's Greek here is the same as Hebrews 1:7, which quotes the Septuagint of Psalm 104:4, so the Plain English Translation uses the site's Hebrews wording. Pneumata can be "winds" or "spirits"; Lake has "spirits." The Hebrew of the psalm reads the other way round: "He makes the winds into his messengers and a blazing fire into his servants" (Psalm 104:4). Hebrews and Clement use the Greek to show that angels are servants, made for God's work, while the Son rules.

a: You are my son
p: Like Hebrews 1:5, Clement quotes Psalm 2:7, and then goes on with Psalm 2:8, which Hebrews does not.
b: The first sentence is Psalm 2:7 as Hebrews 1:5 quotes it: "You are my son. This day I have fathered you" (Hebrews 1:5). Clement then adds Psalm 2:8, in the site's wording, which fits the Greek: "Ask it of me, and I will hand you the nations to inherit, and the far ends of the earth to hold as your own" (Psalm 2:8). The words are spoken "about his Son" by "the Master," God the Father. Acts 13:33 applies Psalm 2:7 to the resurrection.

a: Sit at my right hand
p: The Lord seated at God's right hand, as in Hebrews 1:13 and the Gospels.
b: Clement gives Psalm 110:1 as Hebrews 1:13 does, and the site's Hebrews wording is used. Jesus used it to ask how David's son could be David's Lord (Matthew 22:44), and Peter used it of the risen Christ (Acts 2:34–35).

a: Who, then, are the enemies?
p: Clement answers: those who oppose God's will. In this letter that includes the leaders of the revolt.
b: Hebrews leaves the enemies of Psalm 110 unnamed. Clement names them by their conduct: "the wicked, and those who set themselves against his will." He has just said God "takes his stand against" (antitassetai) the proud (30:2); here the wicked "set themselves against" (antitassomenoi) God's will. The Corinthians would hear the warning: to resist the order God gave the church is to stand among Christ's enemies. Clement still hopes the leaders will repent (57:1).

a: let us serve as soldiers
p: Clement holds up the Roman army as a model of order. He writes from Rome, the capital of that army.
b: The New Testament uses army pictures for the Christian life: "as Christ Jesus' good soldier" (2 Timothy 2:3), the armor of God (Ephesians 6:11–17). Clement goes further and points to the Roman army itself: "our commanders" (37:2), "the emperor" (37:3). Writing from Rome, he can expect his hearers to admire its discipline. His lesson is not about war but about rank: each soldier does his own task under those set over him, and so the whole army works. The church's ranks are the subject of 40–44.

a: prefects, or commanders of a thousand, or of a hundred, or of fifty
p: Roman titles mixed with the ranks of Moses' army in Exodus 18:21.
b: A prefect (eparchos) commanded a large unit or province. The commanders "of a thousand" (chiliarchoi, Roman tribunes) and "of a hundred" (centurions) are the officers the New Testament knows (Acts 21:31; 10:1). "Commanders of fifty" is not a Roman rank. It comes from the Greek Bible: Moses set over the people "captains of thousands, of hundreds, of fifties and of tens" (Exodus 18:21). So Clement's army has a biblical shape. "The emperor" translates basileus, "king," the Greek word for the Roman emperor, as in 1 Peter 2:17, "Give honor to the king" (1 Peter 2:17).

a: a kind of blending
p: Synkrasis: a mixing. Paul says God "blended the body together" (1 Corinthians 12:24).
b: Synkrasis is a mixing or blending, as of wine and water. Paul uses the verb: "God blended the body together and gave extra honor to the part that lacked it" (1 Corinthians 12:24). Clement's sentence moves from the army to the body (37:5), as Paul's chapter does, and both say the great need the small. The Latin version may read this verse a little differently (see the variant).

a: Let us take our body
p: Paul's picture of the church as a body (1 Corinthians 12), and an old Roman story about concord.
b: Clement writes to the church that first heard Paul's picture of the body: "An eye cannot tell a hand, "I can do without you," or a head tell the feet, "I can do without you"" (1 Corinthians 12:21). The picture was also a famous Roman lesson in civic peace. Livy tells how Menenius Agrippa ended a strike of the common people by a fable: the members rebelled against the belly and starved themselves, and so learned that every part serves the others. Livy introduces it as a time when there was "no hope left, save in the concord of the citizens" (Livy, History of Rome 2.32, Spillan's translation). Clement's readers could hear both: the Christian body and the city that must not split.

a: breathe together
p: Sympneō: to breathe together, and so to agree, to grow into one. A word for a united city.
b: Sympneō is to breathe together; by extension it means to agree, to coalesce, to achieve unity, and Plato and Aristotle use it of people who become one community (LSJ). The picture is of a body whose parts share one breath. Clement adds that they share "one submission" (hypotagē mia): every part yields to the good of the whole. That is his cure for Corinth.

a: in keeping with the gift he has been placed in
t: "The gift he has been placed in"
p: Charisma: the gift God gives each member, as in 1 Corinthians 12 and Romans 12.
b: Charisma is a gift of grace. Paul says "Gifts are of many kinds, yet the Spirit is the same" (1 Corinthians 12:4), and 1 Peter 4:10 tells each believer to use the gift he has been given. Clement's phrase is unusual: each one "was placed in" his gift, as a soldier is placed in his rank (37:3). The gift is a post to serve from, and it calls for submission to one's neighbor, not rank over him.

a: Let the rich supply what the poor need
p: The rich give, and the poor give thanks to God for the giver, as in 2 Corinthians 8–9.
b: Clement's rich and poor each have a duty: the rich to supply, the poor to thank God, "who gave him someone through whom his need may be filled." Paul told the Corinthians of the same exchange: "your surplus meets their need" (2 Corinthians 8:14), and the gift "also overflows into many thanks to God" (2 Corinthians 9:12). Clement's word for "need" (hysterēma) is Paul's. The strong caring for the weak recalls Romans 15:1.

a: pure in the flesh
p: Self-control is God's gift, so no one may boast of it. Ignatius gives the same warning.
b: "Pure in the flesh" (hagnos en tē sarki) and "self-control" (enkrateia) here mean sexual purity, probably including the choice not to marry. Paul discussed such choices with the same church (1 Corinthians 7:7, 25–38). Ignatius of Antioch wrote to Polycarp: "If anyone is able to remain in purity for the honor of the Lord's flesh, let him remain so without boasting. Should he boast, he is lost" (Ignatius to Polycarp 5:2). Clement does not say whether anyone at Corinth was boasting of it. His point is that self-control is a gift supplied by God, so no one may boast of it.

a: From what sort of tomb and darkness
t: Out of a tomb and darkness
p: Clement pictures our coming into the world as coming out of a dark grave: the womb, or the earth we were made from.
b: The Greek says only "from what sort of tomb (taphos) and darkness" God brought us into his world. Lightfoot (1890) notes Harnack's pointer to the Greek Psalm 139:15, where the psalmist was made "in the lowest parts of the earth"; the site's Psalm has "embroidered in the lowest parts of the earth" (Psalm 139:15). The "tomb" may be the womb, as Job sets the mother's womb beside his return "there" at death (Job 1:21), or the earth itself, the material the body was made from, since the verse begins "What material were we made from?" Either way the picture links back to the resurrection chapters (24–26): the God who brought us out of one dark place into the light of the world can bring us out of the grave. It also humbles: no one made himself.

a: jeer at us and sneer at us
p: Clement may mean the rebel leaders at Corinth, or proud people in general.
b: Clement does not name the mockers. The words "senseless" and "lift themselves up" repeat 21:5, where "foolish, senseless people" boast in arrogant talk. They may be the leaders of the revolt at Corinth (14:1; 47:6), or proud people in general; the text does not say. The quotation from Job that follows tells them what a mortal's strength is worth.

a: There was no shape before my eyes
p: 39:3–9 is Job 4:16–5:5 from the Greek, the words of Job's friend Eliphaz, with Job 15:15 joined in.
b: The quotation is Eliphaz's night vision and his advice to Job (Job 4:16–5:5), with the Greek line of Job 15:15, that heaven is not pure before God, added at 39:5. Clement follows the Septuagint, which differs from the Hebrew in many lines; the site's Job reads "A figure was there in front of my eyes" (Job 4:16), where the Greek says "there was no shape." At the end of Job, God tells Eliphaz, "You did not say what is right about me, the way my servant Job did" (Job 42:7). Clement still calls these words "written" Scripture, as Paul quotes Eliphaz in 1 Corinthians 3:19 (Job 5:13). Their truth about human weakness stands, even though Eliphaz misapplied it to Job.

a: How much less those who live in houses of clay
p: Clement's Greek has ea de, which Lightfoot renders "how much more"; the main Septuagint manuscripts have only "and."
b: The main Septuagint manuscripts begin Job 4:19 "and those who live in houses of clay." Clement's Greek has ea de, as Codex Alexandrinus of the Septuagint does. Lightfoot (1890) renders Clement's words "how much more, ye that dwell" and the Alexandrinus reading "let alone those that dwell," and notes that Symmachus's Greek has "how much more" (posō mallon), to which ea in this construction is equal. Lake takes it as an exclamation: "Away then, ye who inhabit houses of clay." The Plain English Translation follows Lightfoot's sense: if heaven is not pure, mortals are far less so, "how much less." The Hebrew line asks the same: "Then what of those who live in houses of clay" (Job 4:19). The houses of clay are human bodies, made from the earth (Genesis 2:7; 2 Corinthians 5:1); Lightfoot takes them so.

a: jealousy puts to death
p: Clement's great theme from chapters 3–6 returns in Job's words.
b: The Greek Job 5:2 says "jealousy (zēlos) puts to death the one who has gone astray." It is Clement's own word for the sin that began the trouble at Corinth: in chapters 3–6 jealousy killed Abel, drove Jacob away, and brought death to Peter and Paul. By ending this part of the letter with these lines, Clement lets Scripture say again what he has argued: jealousy and pride destroy the one who holds them.

a: what was prepared for them
p: The Septuagint says "what they gathered"; Clement's Greek says "what was prepared for them."
b: The Septuagint of Job 5:5 reads "what they gathered, the righteous will eat." Clement's Greek has "what was prepared for them." The Hebrew differs again: "Whatever he harvests, the hungry eat" (Job 5:5). Clement's wording turns the line toward God's judgment: what was prepared for the proud goes to the righteous instead. "Mocked" (kolabrizō) is a rare verb; the lexicon knows it in this sense only from this verse of the Greek Job.
